title: Officers who shot knife-wielding schizophrenic man say they would do it again
subtitle: The Toronto police officers who fatally shot a knife-wielding schizophrenic man say they would do it again if put in the same position.
article: The Toronto police officers who fatally shot a knife-wielding schizophrenic man two years ago say they would do it again if put in the same position.
"I've never second-guessed anything I did that night," said Const. John Tanner. "I thought I was going to die."
Tanner was testifying at the inquest into the death of Byron Debassige, a 28-year-old man who battled mental illness, alcoholism and drug addiction throughout his life.

Debassige was shot multiple times in the chest by Tanner and Const. Bradley Coutts after allegedly lunging at the officers with a pocket knife in Oriole Park on Feb. 16, 2008. They were called to the area when Debassige stole two lemons from a Yonge St. market and threatened the store's owners with a knife.
The Special Investigations Unit cleared the officers four months later, saying they had no option but to shoot Debassige.
Coutts said he regrets the incident happened, but does not regret his actions.
"It's not to say I'm unsympathetic to people with problems . . . but (Debassige) didn't give us a choice."

The officers testified they confronted Debassige on the pathway in Oriole Park and asked him to put down the glass juice bottle he was carrying. Instead, Debassige tucked the bottle under his arm and reached into his pocket, pulling out a knife with an eight-centimetre blade, they said. The officers immediately drew their guns and pointed them at Debassige, yelling at him to drop the knife.
"He didn't respond, he just started coming at us at an aggressive pace" from a distance of about six metres, Tanner said.
The officers said they took several steps backwards, yelling at Debassige to stop moving, but he continued in their direction.

When they reached the top of a downward slope, they said they told Debassige to stop or they would shoot. He stopped for a moment, they said, before lunging at them from 1.5 metres away. The entire confrontation lasted only 10 to 15 seconds, the officers testified.

The lawyer representing Debassige's family, Barry Swadron, suggested to Tanner and Coutts that they could have taken a "softer" approach to the situation, and may have considered Debassige had mental illness from the nature of the robbery.
"Did it twig in your mind that an armed robbery for lemons was an unusual thing?" Swadron asked.
"A knife is a knife," Tanner responded.
"A knife can kill you regardless of a guy's mental illness or his impairment."
Outside court, Swadron criticized police training for the lack of preparation in dealing with people with mental illness.
"You can rest assured that if we have the status quo . . . we're going to have more dead people on the streets of Toronto and chances are they're going to be mentally ill."
Both officers testified they had no information about Debassige's mental illness.
The inquest will also delve into police training methods, and Debassige's history with the judicial system and his exposure to mental health services to determine if future deaths can be prevented.
The inquest cannot make any findings of legal responsibility.
